title: 24 Hour Clock Grade 4: Convert, Read Timetables & Find Duration + Free Quiz
meta_title: 24 Hour Clock Grade 4: Convert Time + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Master the 24 hour clock in Grade 4: convert a.m. and p.m. to 24-hour time, read railway timetables and work out elapsed time, with a free quiz.
excerpt: A train that leaves at 14:35 does not confuse a child who understands the 24-hour clock. Here is how I teach Grade 4 to convert times, read a railway timetable, and work out how long a journey takes.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Stand on any platform at a railway station and read the departure board: Rajdhani 16:50, local 17:12, express 19:05. There is no a.m. or p.m. anywhere. That board is the reason the 24 hour clock at Grade 4 matters more than most parents expect — it is not an abstract exercise, it is how India actually tells the time on trains, flights and TV schedules. By Grade 4 a child has already learned to read a clock to the minute in Grade 3. The new job now is the 24-hour system, converting between it and a.m./p.m. time, and working out how long something lasts.

In my experience teaching nine-year-olds, the whole topic hinges on one rule they can say out loud. Get that rule solid and the rest — timetables, durations, even crossing midnight — falls into place.

The one rule of the 24 hour clock for Grade 4

Here it is: for any time in the afternoon or evening, add 12 to the hour. Three o’clock in the afternoon — 3 p.m. — becomes 3 + 12 = 15:00. Nine at night, 9 p.m., becomes 21:00. That is the entire trick. Morning times stay almost the same: 7 a.m. is simply 07:00.

Two spots trip children up, so name them early:

  • Midnight is 00:00 (the day starts over), not 24:00 on most boards.
  • Noon is 12:00, and 12 midnight is 00:00 — the two twelves are opposite ends of the day.
  • The 24-hour clock always shows four digits: 6 a.m. is written 06:00, never 6:00.

Going the other way

To turn a 24-hour time back into a.m./p.m., look at the hour. If it is 13 or more, subtract 12 and add ‘p.m.’ So 13:00 is 1 p.m., 18:45 is 6:45 p.m. If the hour is under 12, it is a.m. (except 12:00, which is noon). I tell students: 13:00 is one o’clock in the afternoon — the very first number past twelve.

A conversion table worth memorising

I ask every Grade 4 class to keep this table in the back of their notebook. After a fortnight of glances, most of them stop needing it.

Reading a railway timetable

Once a child can convert, a timetable stops looking like a wall of numbers. Take a simple one for a bus running Jaipur to Ajmer:

  • Departs Jaipur — 09:20
  • Reaches Kishangarh — 11:05
  • Reaches Ajmer — 11:50

Every entry is a 24-hour time, so there is no guessing morning from evening. The skill to practise is scanning across a row and down a column: which bus reaches Ajmer before noon, which one leaves after 5 p.m. (that is, 17:00 or later). Give a child a real printed timetable and a made-up trip — ‘you must reach the wedding by 18:00, which train do you catch?’ — and the reading becomes a puzzle instead of a chore.

Elapsed time: how long does it take?

This is the part Grade 4 finds hardest, and the mistake is almost always the same. Children subtract 11:50 − 09:20 as if minutes worked like ordinary numbers and get 2 hours 30 minutes. Time does not carry in tens; it carries in sixties. So I never teach column subtraction for duration. I teach counting on, the same idea they used for addition years earlier.

To find the journey from 09:20 to 11:50, count in friendly hops:

  • 09:20 to 10:00 is 40 minutes
  • 10:00 to 11:00 is 1 hour
  • 11:00 to 11:50 is 50 minutes
  • Total: 1 hour + 40 + 50 minutes = 1 hour 90 minutes = 2 hours 30 minutes

Crossing noon and midnight

The counting-on method quietly handles the trickiest case — a duration that runs past noon or midnight — because you never subtract across the join. From 22:40 to 00:10 you hop 22:40 to 23:00 (20 min), 23:00 to 00:00 (1 hour), 00:00 to 00:10 (10 min): 1 hour 30 minutes. Try doing that with column subtraction and watch the confusion. Counting on wins every time.

A weekly routine that sticks

Ten minutes most days beats a long Sunday drill. What has worked for parents I know: two days converting real times off the TV guide, two days reading an actual timetable, and one day on ‘how long until…’ questions using the kitchen clock. Keep the numbers real — the cricket match starts at 19:30, dinner at 20:15, so how long is the wait? Children who practise on real events remember the 24 hour clock long after the worksheet is gone.

One honest caveat: do not rush a child onto elapsed-time questions before conversion is automatic. A child still counting on fingers to add 12 will drown in a two-step duration problem. Solid conversion first, durations second.

Try the quiz, then the printable worksheet

Below is a free eight-question quiz covering exactly what we have looked at — converting a.m./p.m. to the 24 hour clock, reading a timetable and finding elapsed time. quiz.title: Grade 4 24 Hour Clock Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on converting times, reading a timetable and working out duration. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: What is 3 p.m. on the 24-hour clock?
questions.explanation: For afternoon and evening times, add 12 to the hour: 3 + 12 = 15, so 3 p.m. is 15:00.
Morning times stay the same, but the 24-hour clock uses four digits, so 7:30 a.m. is written 07:30.

questions.q: What time is 21:00 in a.m./p.m. form?
questions.explanation: The hour is more than 12, so subtract 12: 21 − 12 = 9, and it is evening, giving 9 p.m.

questions.q: How is midnight usually shown on a 24-hour clock?
questions.explanation: Midnight starts a new day, so it is 00:00. Noon, not midnight, is 12:00.

questions.q: A train leaves at 14:00. That is the same as:
questions.explanation: 14 − 12 = 2, and the hour is past noon, so 14:00 is 2 p.m.

questions.q: A bus departs at 09:15 and arrives at 09:50. How long is the trip?
questions.explanation: Count on from 09:15 to 09:50: that is 35 minutes.

questions.q: How long is a journey from 10:40 to 12:10?
questions.explanation: Hop 10:40 to 11:00 (20 min), 11:00 to 12:00 (1 hour), 12:00 to 12:10 (10 min): total 1 hour 30 minutes.

questions.q: The timetable shows a film starting at 18:45. When is that?
questions.explanation: 18 − 12 = 6, and it is evening, so 18:45 is 6:45 p.m.

faq.q: How do you explain the 24-hour clock to a Grade 4 child?
faq.a: Start with one rule: for afternoon and evening times, add 12 to the hour, so 3 p.m. becomes 15:00. Morning times stay the same but use four digits, like 07:00. Practise on real times from a TV guide or railway board so it feels useful, not abstract.

faq.q: Why does India use the 24-hour clock on trains?
faq.a: Railway and airline timetables use the 24-hour clock so there is no chance of mixing up morning and evening — 5:00 could mean two things, but 05:00 and 17:00 never clash. That is why learning it in Grade 4 has a real, everyday payoff.

faq.q: What is the easiest way to work out how long something takes?
faq.a: Count on in friendly hops rather than subtracting. From 09:20 to 11:50, jump to the next hour, count whole hours, then the last minutes: 40 min + 1 hour + 50 min = 2 hours 30 minutes. This avoids the classic mistake of treating minutes like ordinary tens.

faq.q: What time is 13:00 and why is it not 3 o’clock?
faq.a: 13:00 is 1 p.m. — the first hour past noon. It is easy to misread the 3 in 13, so remind the child to subtract 12 from any hour of 13 or more: 13 − 12 = 1.
